newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PARLIAMENT STARTS 1997 BUDGET DEBATE.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PARLIAMENT STARTS 1997 BUDGET DEBATE.

text.p: Poland's lower house of parliament on Thursday began a debate on next year's budget draft amid uncertainty over the 1997 tax levels.

Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko told the house the draft, expected to be sent to committees for scrutiny later this week, envisaged real growth in spending and revenues, possible thanks to an expected 5.5-percent increase of gross domestic product.
"This is a budget of social preferences, constructed for the people," he said.

The government submitted its draft on October 28 and the house has three months since then to analyse the draft and propose changes before it is sent to the Senate and the president for final approval.
Kolodko was speaking before the Senate's vote later on Thursday or on Friday on personal income tax bills, which split the ruling coalition of ex-communists and a peasant party.
Kolodko said that if the taxes stayed on this year's levels of 21, 33 and 45 percent, the budget deficit would shrink to 2.6 percent of GDP from 2.8 percent planned for 1996.
Kolodko and coalition's ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) has earlier recommended lowering the taxation to 20, 31 and 43 percent, which would entail a deficit of 2.8 percent of GDP.
But last month the Peasants helped the opposition to push through in the lower house a four-level tax scale of 17, 20, 33 and 45 percent, which the finance ministry said were not economically viable.

Senate committees proposed to cut taxes to 20, 32 and 44 percent and Kolodko said on Wednesday the government was ready to accept the solution. The Senate will be also choosign this week from several other proposals.
Kolodko said that regardless of the tax scale, cutting year-on-year inflation to 13 percent in December next year from 17.8 percent expected this year would be the government priority.
"We will be determined to take actions, if parliament permits, aimed at bringing inflation to no more than 13 percent in December 1997..." Kolodko said.
Central bank president Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz urged parliament on Thursday to approve the lowest possible deficit.
She said any gap higher that 2.3 percent would mean either more a more restrictive monetary policy next year or foresaking government's macroeconomic targets.
The government draft increases spending by 2.3 percent in real terms to 127.7 billion zlotys and revenues by 2.8 percent to 116.4 billion zlotys.
Health care system, education, culture, telecommunications, the state administration and defense will see the highest rises in spending.
The revenues would include a 3.5 billion zloty income from privatisation.
Out of the 11.3 billion gap about 6.7 billion zlotys would be financed in the domestic banking sector.
